topic: The Stanford prison experiment and why it's disputed
title: The Stanford Prison Experiment and Why It's Disputed
voiceover: Did ordinary students really turn into cruel guards in a mock prison? In 1971, Philip Zimbardo's team at Stanford ran a simulated prison study with 24 selected male students. Ten became prisoners and eleven became guards. It was planned for two weeks but ended after six days. In 2019, Thibault Le Texier analyzed archival records and argued the guards had been coached. He reported they were told which behavior was wanted. In a BBC replication reported in 2006, Stephen Reicher and Alexander Haslam found the guards did not identify with their role. These are the authors' reported findings, and the original team defended its study. So this famous experiment is now seriously disputed, and does not simply show that situations make people cruel. Tomorrow: why do people gossip so much?

A 2019 archival analysis argued the guards had been coached, and a BBC replication reported guards did not identify strongly with their role. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Haney, C., Banks, C., & Zimbardo, P. (1973). Interpersonal dynamics in a simulated prison. International Journal of Criminology and Penology, 1, 69-97. Source: Le Texier, T. (2019). accuracy_note: The video presents the criticisms as reported by the authors (Le Texier 2019; Reicher & Haslam 2006), not as settled fact. Zimbardo and colleagues defended the study. Haney et al. figures come from secondary summaries.
